literature.headline_zh: 人腺病毒本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期人腺病毒研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 3D 分析显示核内包涵体是病毒颗粒在细胞内积聚的主要部位。在核内包涵体内鉴定出病毒颗粒,并以与该包涵体的纤维结构平行的晶体结构排列。此外,成熟的病毒颗粒主要分布在核内包涵体周围。 [10.3390/ijms27209181]
与 A549 上皮细胞相比,每个细胞的淋巴细胞需要大约 10 至 20 倍的 Ad5F35 颗粒才能达到相似的转导水平。定量结果显示,原代 NK 细胞每 μm2 大约有 100 个 CD46 分子,而 HeLa 细胞每 μm2 大约有 2000 个 CD46,差异达 20 倍。 [10.3390/ijms27209183]

hCD46 人源化小鼠在 HAdV-7 感染后表现出肺部病毒负荷增加、感染性病毒粒子可恢复以及肺部病理更加严重。单细胞分析揭示了常驻肺泡巨噬细胞的消耗、炎症巨噬细胞亚群的扩张以及淋巴转录状态的重塑。这些变化伴随着显着的 I/II 型干扰素和干扰素相关趋化因子程序。B 细胞、CD4+ 和 CD8+ T 细胞显示 ISG 相关转录状态,以及选定的效应器和记忆相关程序的改变。 [10.3389/fimmu.2026.1919716]
与基于 人腺病毒 的 媒介 相比,PAdV 宿主 可能在 宿主 关联、兽医相关性和粘膜递送方面提供潜在优势,同时避免直接依赖常见的 人腺病毒 主干。 [10.3390/ani16203247]

papers.title: Human CD46 humanized mice reveal interferon associated pulmonary immune remodeling during human adenovirus type 7 lung infection
papers.abstract: Background Human adenovirus type 7(HAdV-7) is a major cause of severe pediatric pneumonia, but the mechanisms linking viral infection to pulmonary immune remodeling and lung pathology remain incompletely understood. Progress has been limited by the lack of physiologically relevant animal models that recapitulate human susceptibility. Methods We generated human CD46 (hCD46) humanized mice and evaluated pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lung tissues from wild type and hCD46 humanized mice under control and infected conditions to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, and intercellular communication. Human PBMC bulk transcriptomes from pediatric HAdV infection were further analyzed to assess the systemic relevance of mouse lung derived immune programs. Results hCD46 humanized mice showed increased pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virions, and more severe lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell profiling revealed depletion of resident alveolar macrophages, pronounced expansion of inflammatory macrophage subsets, and remodeling of lymphoid transcriptional states in infected hCD46 lungs. These changes were accompanied by prominent type I/II interferon and interferon associated chemokine programs. B cells and CD4 + and CD8 + T cells showed prominent interferon stimulated genes (ISGs) associated transcriptional states, together with alterations in selected effector- and memory-associated programs and computationally inferred trajectories. Projection of mouse lung derived signatures onto transcriptomes of human peripheral blood mononuclear cell showed that selected interferon associated myeloid and lymphoid programs were also detectable systemically in pediatric HAdV infection. Conclusions HAdV-7 infection in hCD46 humanized mice was associated with an interferon enriched pulmonary inflammatory environment, prominent inflammatory myeloid remodeling, and altered lymphoid transcriptional states. This susceptible mouse model provides a useful experimental tool for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and for preclinical evaluation of antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the mechanisms linking human adenovirus type 7 (HAdV-7) infection to pulmonary immune remodeling and lung pathology in children, addressing the limitations of current animal models.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used human CD46 (hCD46) humanized mice to evaluate pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection, with analysis performed on lung tissues and systemic immune programs.
analysis.methods: Human CD46 humanized mice were generated and infected with HAdV-7. Pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology were assessed. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lung tissues to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, and intercellular communication. Systemic relevance was further analyzed using human PBMC transcriptomes.
analysis.main_results: hCD46 humanized mice showed increased pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virions, and more severe lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell profiling revealed depletion of resident alveolar macrophages, expansion of inflammatory macrophage subsets, and remodeling of lymphoid transcriptional states. These changes were accompanied by prominent type I/II interferon and interferon-associated chemokine programs. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study concluded that HAdV-7 infection in hCD46 humanized mice was associated with an interferon-enriched pulmonary inflammatory environment, prominent inflammatory myeloid remodeling, and altered lymphoid transcriptional states, providing a useful model for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and preclinical evaluation of antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the hCD46 humanized mouse model can be used to study HAdV-7 associated lung disease and to evaluate antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies, enhancing our understanding of the disease mechanisms and potential therapeutic interventions.

analysis.summary_en: This study used human CD46 humanized mice to evaluate HAdV-7 infection, showing increased pulmonary viral burden, interferon-enriched inflammation, and immune cell remodeling. The findings suggest a useful model for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and evaluating therapeutic strategies.

analysis_en.methods: Human CD46 humanized mice were generated and infected with HAdV-7. Pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology were assessed. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lung tissues to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, and intercellular communication. Systemic relevance was further analyzed using human PBMC transcriptomes.
analysis_en.main_results: hCD46 humanized mice showed increased pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virions, and more severe lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell profiling revealed depletion of resident alveolar macrophages, expansion of inflammatory macrophage subsets, and remodeling of lymphoid transcriptional states. These changes were accompanied by prominent type I/II interferon and interferon-associated chemokine programs. B cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells showed ISGs associated transcriptional states, with alterations in selected effector- and memory-associated programs.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The study concluded that HAdV-7 infection in hCD46 humanized mice was associated with an interferon-enriched pulmonary inflammatory environment, prominent inflammatory myeloid remodeling, and altered lymphoid transcriptional states, providing a useful model for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and preclinical evaluation of antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies.

papers.title_zh: 人 CD46 人源化小鼠揭示 人腺病毒 7 型肺部感染期间干扰素相关的肺部免疫重塑
papers.source_body_en: Background Human adenovirus type 7(HAdV-7) is a major cause of severe pediatric pneumonia, but the mechanisms linking viral infection to pulmonary immune remodeling and lung pathology remain incompletely understood. Progress has been limited by the lack of physiologically relevant animal models that recapitulate human susceptibility. Methods We generated human CD46 (hCD46) humanized mice and evaluated pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virus, and lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on lung tissues from wild type and hCD46 humanized mice under control and infected conditions to characterize cellular composition, transcriptional states, and intercellular communication. Human PBMC bulk transcriptomes from pediatric HAdV infection were further analyzed to assess the systemic relevance of mouse lung derived immune programs. Results hCD46 humanized mice showed increased pulmonary viral burden, recoverable infectious virions, and more severe lung pathology after HAdV-7 infection. Single-cell profiling revealed depletion of resident alveolar macrophages, pronounced expansion of inflammatory macrophage subsets, and remodeling of lymphoid transcriptional states in infected hCD46 lungs. These changes were accompanied by prominent type I/II interferon and interferon associated chemokine programs. B cells and CD4 + and CD8 + T cells showed prominent interferon stimulated genes (ISGs) associated transcriptional states, together with alterations in selected effector- and memory-associated programs and computationally inferred trajectories. Projection of mouse lung derived signatures onto transcriptomes of human peripheral blood mononuclear cell showed that selected interferon associated myeloid and lymphoid programs were also detectable systemically in pediatric HAdV infection. Conclusions HAdV-7 infection in hCD46 humanized mice was associated with an interferon enriched pulmonary inflammatory environment, prominent inflammatory myeloid remodeling, and altered lymphoid transcriptional states. This susceptible mouse model provides a useful experimental tool for studying HAdV-7 associated lung disease and for preclinical evaluation of antiviral, immunomodulatory, and vaccine strategies.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景 人腺病毒 7 型(HAdV-7)是严重小儿肺炎的主要原因,但病毒感染与肺部免疫重塑和肺部病理学之间的联系机制仍不完全清楚。由于缺乏概括人类易感性的生理相关动物模型,进展受到限制。方法 我们生成人 CD46 (hCD46) 人源化小鼠,并评估 HAdV-7 感染后的肺部病毒负荷、可恢复的感染性病毒和肺部病理学。在对照和感染条件下对野生型和 hCD46 人源化小鼠的肺组织进行单细胞 RNA 测序,以表征细胞组成、转录状态和细胞间通讯。进一步分析了儿科 HAdV 感染的人 PBMC 大量转录组,以评估小鼠肺源性免疫程序的系统相关性。结果 hCD46 人源化小鼠在 HAdV-7 感染后表现出肺部病毒负荷增加、感染性病毒粒子可恢复以及肺部病理更加严重。单细胞分析揭示了受感染 hCD46 肺中常驻肺泡巨噬细胞的消耗、炎症巨噬细胞亚群的显着扩张以及淋巴转录状态的重塑。这些变化伴随着显着的 I/II 型干扰素和干扰素相关趋化因子程序。B 细胞以及 CD4 + 和 CD8 + T 细胞显示出与干扰素刺激基因 (ISG) 相关的显着转录状态,以及选定的效应器和记忆相关程序以及计算推断轨迹的变化。将小鼠肺源性特征投射到人外周血单核细胞的转录组上表明,在儿科 HAdV 感染中也可以系统地检测到选定的干扰素相关的骨髓和淋巴程序。结论 hCD46 人源化小鼠中的 HAdV-7 感染与富含干扰素的肺部炎症环境、显着的炎症骨髓重塑和淋巴转录状态改变有关。这种易感小鼠模型为研究 HAdV-7 相关肺部疾病以及 抗病毒药物、免疫调节和 疫苗 策略的临床前评估提供了有用的实验工具。

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Intranuclear Inclusion Body and Virus Formation in Human Adenovirus Type 5-Infected Cells
papers.abstract: Human adenovirus type 5 (HAdV-5) forms a characteristic intranuclear inclusion body in infected cells. However, the relationship between the intranuclear inclusion body and virus formation in HAdV-5-infected cells remains unclear. This study conducted a detailed investigation of the relationship between the structure of the inclusion body and the localization of the virus in HAdV-5-infected cells using electron microscopy and three-dimensional (3D) tomography analytical techniques. Immunostaining for viral proteins was also performed to determine their colocalization with the intranuclear inclusion body. 3D analysis revealed the intranuclear inclusion body as the major site of viral particle accumulation in the cells. Viral particles were identified within the intranuclear inclusion body and arranged in a crystalline structure parallel to the fibrous structures of this body. Moreover, mature viral particles were predominantly distributed around the intranuclear inclusion body. Certain viral proteins were also detected in the intranuclear inclusion body by immunoelectron microscopy. We propose that intranuclear inclusion bodies serve as sites of viral replication in HAdV-5-infected cells. Through the 3D analysis, we clarified the relationship between the distribution and localization of intranuclear inclusion bodies and viral particles in HAdV-5-infected cells. These findings can improve our understanding of adenoviral infection mechanisms and may contribute toward developing novel antiviral strategies.

papers.title_zh: 人腺病毒 5 型感染细胞核内包涵体和病毒形成的时空分析
papers.source_body_en: Human adenovirus type 5 (HAdV-5) forms a characteristic intranuclear inclusion body in infected cells. However, the relationship between the intranuclear inclusion body and virus formation in HAdV-5-infected cells remains unclear. This study conducted a detailed investigation of the relationship between the structure of the inclusion body and the localization of the virus in HAdV-5-infected cells using electron microscopy and three-dimensional (3D) tomography analytical techniques. Immunostaining for viral proteins was also performed to determine their colocalization with the intranuclear inclusion body. 3D analysis revealed the intranuclear inclusion body as the major site of viral particle accumulation in the cells. Viral particles were identified within the intranuclear inclusion body and arranged in a crystalline structure parallel to the fibrous structures of this body. Moreover, mature viral particles were predominantly distributed around the intranuclear inclusion body. Certain viral proteins were also detected in the intranuclear inclusion body by immunoelectron microscopy. We propose that intranuclear inclusion bodies serve as sites of viral replication in HAdV-5-infected cells. Through the 3D analysis, we clarified the relationship between the distribution and localization of intranuclear inclusion bodies and viral particles in HAdV-5-infected cells. These findings can improve our understanding of adenoviral infection mechanisms and may contribute toward developing novel antiviral strategies.

papers.title: Porcine Adenovirus-Based Viral Vectors for Swine Vaccines: A Scoping Review and Future Perspectives
papers.abstract: Porcine adenoviruses (PAdVs) are promising but still underdeveloped viral-vector platforms for swine vaccine development. Compared with human adenovirus-based vectors, PAdV vectors may offer potential advantages in host association, veterinary relevance, and mucosal delivery while avoiding direct reliance on common human adenovirus backbones. This review summarizes current knowledge on PAdV biology, vector engineering, vaccine applications, immune responses, translational challenges, and future priorities. Early studies showed that recombinant PAdV vectors can express heterologous antigens from important swine pathogens, including classical swine fever virus, pseudorabies virus, and transmissible gastroenteritis virus. The strongest direct proof-of-concept evidence comes from recombinant PAdV expressing classical swine fever virus E2/gp55, which induced neutralizing antibodies and protection in pigs. Comparative adenovirus-vectored swine vaccine studies support the broader feasibility of adenoviral antigen delivery for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, porcine epidemic diarrhea, swine influenza, and African swine fever, but these data should not be interpreted as direct validation of PAdV for these diseases. Major gaps remain in anti-PAdV immunity, genetic stability, biosafety, shedding, target-animal safety, DIVA compatibility, manufacturing, and regulatory readiness. Recent advances in PAdV-5 reverse genetics provide new opportunities for modern vector design.

papers.title_zh: 用于猪的基于猪腺病毒的病毒 媒介:范围界定回顾和未来展望
papers.source_body_en: Porcine adenoviruses (PAdVs) are promising but still underdeveloped viral-vector platforms for swine vaccine development. Compared with human adenovirus-based vectors, PAdV vectors may offer potential advantages in host association, veterinary relevance, and mucosal delivery while avoiding direct reliance on common human adenovirus backbones. This review summarizes current knowledge on PAdV biology, vector engineering, vaccine applications, immune responses, translational challenges, and future priorities. Early studies showed that recombinant PAdV vectors can express heterologous antigens from important swine pathogens, including classical swine fever virus, pseudorabies virus, and transmissible gastroenteritis virus. The strongest direct proof-of-concept evidence comes from recombinant PAdV expressing classical swine fever virus E2/gp55, which induced neutralizing antibodies and protection in pigs. Comparative adenovirus-vectored swine vaccine studies support the broader feasibility of adenoviral antigen delivery for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, porcine epidemic diarrhea, swine influenza, and African swine fever, but these data should not be interpreted as direct validation of PAdV for these diseases. Major gaps remain in anti-PAdV immunity, genetic stability, biosafety, shedding, target-animal safety, DIVA compatibility, manufacturing, and regulatory readiness. Recent advances in PAdV-5 reverse genetics provide new opportunities for modern vector design.

papers.title: Targeting of Immune Cells by Human Adenoviruses: CD46 Receptor Density Influences Entry of Chimaeric Ad5F35 into Natural Killer Cells
papers.abstract: Most adenovirus (Ad) vectors are based on the genome of human Ad type 5 (Ad5), which targets their entry to cells that express the Coxsackie and adenovirus receptor (CAR or CXADR). However, certain human Ads do not use CAR; for example, Ad35 interacts with cell surface CD46 and Ad3 uses desmoglein 2 (DSG2) for cell entry. In this study, a comparison of different Ad receptors using transcriptomic and proteomic databases showed that CD46 is widely expressed across human cells and tissues whereas CAR and DSG2 are more restricted to epithelial cells. We have used a hybrid virus, Ad5F35, that comprises an Ad5 genome in which the Ad5 fibre was replaced with that of Ad35, thus retargeting the virus from CAR- to CD46-expressing cells and enabling transduction of primary human NK and T cells. However, lymphocytes required approximately 10-to-20-fold-more Ad5F35 particles per cell (ppc) compared to A549 epithelial cells to achieve a similar level of transduction. Consistent with this, quantitation of the cell-surface density of CD46 molecules revealed approximately 100 CD46 molecules per μm2 in primary NK cells compared with approximately 2000 CD46 per μm2 in HeLa cells, a 20-fold difference. Cell surface CD46 density was reduced by approximately 95% by RNA interference in HeLa cells to levels that approximate those found on NK cells. Lower CD46 density reduced transduction by Ad5F35 but this could be compensated for with increased MOI. Our results identify the density of cell surface CD46 as a critical determinant of Ad5F35 transduction and demonstrate that Ad5F35 is an efficient vector for gene delivery in primary human NK cells.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate how the density of the CD46 receptor influences the entry of chimaeric Ad5F35 virus into natural killer cells, addressing the gap in understanding the relationship between receptor density and viral transduction efficiency.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a comparison of different adenovirus receptors using transcriptomic and proteomic databases, and tested the transduction efficiency of Ad5F35 in primary human NK cells and A549 epithelial cells.
analysis.methods: The researchers utilized a hybrid virus, Ad5F35, which incorporates the Ad35 fibre into the Ad5 genome, and employed RNA interference to reduce CD46 density in HeLa cells, enabling a direct comparison of transduction efficiency across cell types.
analysis.main_results: Lymphocytes required approximately 10-to-20-fold more Ad5F35 particles per cell compared to A549 epithelial cells to achieve similar transduction levels. analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that CD46 receptor density is a critical factor in determining the efficiency of Ad5F35 transduction, highlighting the importance of receptor density in viral entry mechanisms.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results have implications for the development of adenoviral vectors for gene delivery in primary human NK cells, potentially improving the efficacy of gene therapy applications targeting these cells.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on transcriptomic and proteomic databases and the use of RNA interference to manipulate CD46 density, which may not fully represent in vivo conditions. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these constraints.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how the density of the CD46 receptor influences the transduction efficiency of the chimaeric Ad5F35 virus in primary human NK cells compared to A549 epithelial cells. Using a hybrid virus with Ad35 fibre and RNA interference to reduce CD46 levels in HeLa cells, the researchers found that NK cells have significantly lower CD46 density than epithelial cells, requiring 10-to-20-fold more Ad5F35 particles for similar transduction levels. The results highlight CD46 density as a critical determinant of Ad5F35 entry and suggest its potential utility in gene delivery applications targeting NK cells. However, the study's reliance on databases and RNA interference introduces limitations, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

papers.title: A novel adenovirus 19K/IX protein enhances infection by attenuating proteasomal degradation of tyrosine-ubiquitinated capsid protein IX
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are double-stranded DNA viruses that cause a wide range of diseases, including respiratory, ocular, and gastrointestinal infections. HAdVs rely extensively on alternative splicing to expand their coding capacity and regulate gene expression during infection. Using replication-competent epitope-tagged HAdV-C5 viruses, we investigated the function of a newly identified alternatively spliced viral transcript, 19K/IX, derived from the E1B19K and pIX genes. We show that the 19K/IX protein binds to and stabilizes the minor capsid protein IX (pIX), thereby attenuating its proteasomal degradation and enhancing the production of infectious viral progeny. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that pIX degradation is mediated by non-canonical ubiquitination of the conserved tyrosine residues Y14 and Y49, which confer pIX subnuclear localization and partially mediate its interaction with the PSMC3 subunit of the 26S proteasome. Collectively, our study identifies 19K/IX as a novel regulator of HAdV-C5 infection and suggests that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination contributes to the regulation of capsid protein IX stability. IMPORTANCE: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are clinically important pathogens and widely used as therapeutic tools. Because of their compact genomes, HAdVs use their genetic information very efficiently through alternative pre-mRNA processing. Here, we describe and characterize 19K/IX, a novel fusion protein generated by alternative splicing of two viral genes during infection. We demonstrate that 19K/IX stabilizes capsid protein IX by preventing its degradation, revealing a previously unrecognized strategy by which HAdVs ensure efficient production of new virus particles. These findings deepen our understanding of HAdV-C5 gene regulation and protein homeostasis and highlight the functional importance of non-canonical HAdV transcripts.

The research addresses the need to understand how HAdVs use alternative splicing to expand their coding capacity and regulate gene expression during infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used replication-competent epitope-tagged HAdV-C5 viruses to investigate the function of the 19K/IX protein. The research was conducted in vitro, focusing on the interaction between the 19K/IX protein and the minor capsid protein IX (pIX) in HAdV-C5 infection.
analysis.methods: They demonstrated that the 19K/IX protein binds to and stabilizes pIX, thereby attenuating its proteasomal degradation and enhancing the production of infectious viral progeny. The study involved molecular biology techniques, including protein-protein interaction assays and ubiquitination analysis.
analysis.main_results: Mechanistically, pIX degradation is mediated by non-canonical ubiquitination of conserved tyrosine residues Y14 and Y49, which confer pIX subnuclear localization and partially mediate its interaction with the PSMC3 subunit of the 26S proteasome.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study identifies 19K/IX as a novel regulator of HAdV-C5 infection and suggests that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination contributes to the regulation of capsid protein IX stability. This finding deepens our understanding of HAdV-C5 gene regulation and protein homeostasis and highlights the functional importance of non-canonical HAdV transcripts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination plays a role in the regulation of capsid protein IX stability, which could have implications for understanding HAdV-C5 infection and potentially for developing therapeutic strategies against HAdV infections.

papers.title_zh: 一种新型腺病毒 19K/IX 蛋白通过减弱酪氨酸泛素化衣壳蛋白 IX 的蛋白酶体降解来增强感染
papers.source_body_en: UNLABELLED: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are double-stranded DNA viruses that cause a wide range of diseases, including respiratory, ocular, and gastrointestinal infections. HAdVs rely extensively on alternative splicing to expand their coding capacity and regulate gene expression during infection. Using replication-competent epitope-tagged HAdV-C5 viruses, we investigated the function of a newly identified alternatively spliced viral transcript, 19K/IX, derived from the E1B19K and pIX genes. We show that the 19K/IX protein binds to and stabilizes the minor capsid protein IX (pIX), thereby attenuating its proteasomal degradation and enhancing the production of infectious viral progeny. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that pIX degradation is mediated by non-canonical ubiquitination of the conserved tyrosine residues Y14 and Y49, which confer pIX subnuclear localization and partially mediate its interaction with the PSMC3 subunit of the 26S proteasome. Collectively, our study identifies 19K/IX as a novel regulator of HAdV-C5 infection and suggests that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination contributes to the regulation of capsid protein IX stability. IMPORTANCE: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are clinically important pathogens and widely used as therapeutic tools. Because of their compact genomes, HAdVs use their genetic information very efficiently through alternative pre-mRNA processing. Here, we describe and characterize 19K/IX, a novel fusion protein generated by alternative splicing of two viral genes during infection. We demonstrate that 19K/IX stabilizes capsid protein IX by preventing its degradation, revealing a previously unrecognized strategy by which HAdVs ensure efficient production of new virus particles. These findings deepen our understanding of HAdV-C5 gene regulation and protein homeostasis and highlight the functional importance of non-canonical HAdV transcripts.

papers.title: Highly neutralizing anti–IFN-ω autoantibodies underlie severe pediatric adenovirus infection
papers.abstract: Neutralizing autoantibodies (auto-Abs) against type I IFNs (IFN-α and IFN-ω) have emerged as major acquired risk factors for severe viral infections. Human adenovirus (HAdV) is highly prevalent in children and can cause severe pneumonia, but the host determinants of disease severity remain poorly understood. We describe here a 5-year-old child with life-threatening HAdV-B7 pneumonia requiring intensive care who carried high-titer anti–IFN-ω auto-Abs of the IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells produced normal amounts of IFN-α and IFN-ω ex vivo; however, IFN-ω was undetectable in the plasma during acute illness. Functional assays demonstrated that the patient’s plasma strongly neutralized IFN-ω, abolishing its antiviral signaling and protective effects, resulting in high levels of adenovirus replication and virus-induced cytotoxicity. These findings implicate anti–IFN-ω auto-Abs in severe adenoviral infection and support immunological screening of pediatric patients with unexplained severe viral pneumonia, which may guide targeted management.

papers.title_zh: 高度中和性抗 IFN-ω 自身抗体是严重儿科腺病毒感染的基础
papers.source_body_en: Neutralizing autoantibodies (auto-Abs) against type I IFNs (IFN-α and IFN-ω) have emerged as major acquired risk factors for severe viral infections. Human adenovirus (HAdV) is highly prevalent in children and can cause severe pneumonia, but the host determinants of disease severity remain poorly understood. We describe here a 5-year-old child with life-threatening HAdV-B7 pneumonia requiring intensive care who carried high-titer anti–IFN-ω auto-Abs of the IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells produced normal amounts of IFN-α and IFN-ω ex vivo; however, IFN-ω was undetectable in the plasma during acute illness. Functional assays demonstrated that the patient’s plasma strongly neutralized IFN-ω, abolishing its antiviral signaling and protective effects, resulting in high levels of adenovirus replication and virus-induced cytotoxicity. These findings implicate anti–IFN-ω auto-Abs in severe adenoviral infection and support immunological screening of pediatric patients with unexplained severe viral pneumonia, which may guide targeted management.
papers.abstract_zh: 针对 I 型干扰素(IFN-α 和 IFN-ω)的中和自身抗体(auto-Abs)已成为严重病毒感染的主要获得性危险因素。人腺病毒 (HAdV) 在​​儿童中非常流行,可引起严重肺炎,但对疾病严重程度的 宿主 决定因素仍知之甚少。我们在此描述了一名 5 岁儿童,患有危及生命的 HAdV-B7 肺炎,需要重症监护,该儿童携带 IgG1 和 IgG3 亚类的高滴度抗 IFN-ω 自身抗体。外周血单核细胞离体产生正常量的IFN-α和IFN-ω;然而,在急性疾病期间,血浆中检测不到 IFN-ω。功能分析表明,患者的血浆强烈中和了 IFN-ω,消除了其 抗病毒药物 信号传导和保护作用,导致高水平的腺病毒复制和病毒诱导的细胞毒性。这些发现表明抗IFN-ω自身抗体与严重腺病毒感染有关,并支持对不明原因严重病毒性肺炎儿科患者进行免疫学筛查,这可能指导有针对性的治疗。

papers.title: Hemagglutinin and fusion proteins precede measles virus ribonucleoproteins and marshal cell-to-cell spread in airway epithelium.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Measles virus (MeV) is the most contagious human respiratory pathogen. To understand how it spreads in the airways, we infected well-differentiated primary cultures of human airway epithelial cells (HAE). We discovered that the MeV attachment protein (hemagglutinin, H), the fusion (F) protein, and the assembly organizer protein (matrix, M) reach newly infected cells ahead of, and independently from, the replicative complex proteins. To characterize the mechanisms of MeV spread, we generated a replication-deficient adenoviral vector expressing the MeV M, F, and H proteins in a doxycycline-inducible manner. This viral vector formed infectious centers that preserved epithelial function like those from MeV infection. To further dissect this process, we generated Ad vectors expressing individual MeV proteins, termed Ad-M, Ad-F, and Ad-H. Transduction of HAE with single, double, and triple Ad vector combinations revealed that Ad-F and Ad-H are necessary and sufficient to form MeV-like infectious centers. MeV enters and spreads within airway epithelia via H protein binding to adherens junction protein, nectin-4. To disrupt spread, we introduced the point mutation H Y543A , a mutation previously described to inhibit nectin-4 binding, in the Ad-H vector. Co-transduction of Ad-F and Ad-H Y543A did not result in MeV-like infectious center formation. Finally, we assessed whether the MeV-related paramyxovirus Nipah (NiV) attachment and fusion proteins (G and F, respectively) support cell-to-cell spread. Co-transduction of HAE with Ad-NiV-G and Ad-NiV-F did not result in infectious center formation, suggesting that decoupling of the membrane fusion apparatus function from replication is a unique feature of the MeV envelope glycoproteins. IMPORTANCE Measles virus is a highly contagious pathogen. We characterized a mechanism by which measles virus spreads rapidly through the cells that line the human airway in an ex vivo model. We show that the proteins of the viral membrane fusion apparatus, hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F), move independently from and reach newly infected cells before the proteins of the replicative complex. Thus, viral protein spread is assembled and arranged in order (i.e., marshaled ). Using adenovirus-based vectors, we show that co-expression of H and F proteins promotes rapid sequential spread to multiple cells and the formation of infectious centers. Further elucidation of the mechanism of measles virus amplification and cell-to-cell spread within the lung may help explain its highly contagious nature.

papers.title_zh: 血凝素和融合蛋白先于麻疹病毒核糖核蛋白出现,并在气道上皮中引导细胞间的传播。
papers.source_body_en: ABSTRACT Measles virus (MeV) is the most contagious human respiratory pathogen. To understand how it spreads in the airways, we infected well-differentiated primary cultures of human airway epithelial cells (HAE). We discovered that the MeV attachment protein (hemagglutinin, H), the fusion (F) protein, and the assembly organizer protein (matrix, M) reach newly infected cells ahead of, and independently from, the replicative complex proteins. To characterize the mechanisms of MeV spread, we generated a replication-deficient adenoviral vector expressing the MeV M, F, and H proteins in a doxycycline-inducible manner. This viral vector formed infectious centers that preserved epithelial function like those from MeV infection. To further dissect this process, we generated Ad vectors expressing individual MeV proteins, termed Ad-M, Ad-F, and Ad-H. Transduction of HAE with single, double, and triple Ad vector combinations revealed that Ad-F and Ad-H are necessary and sufficient to form MeV-like infectious centers. MeV enters and spreads within airway epithelia via H protein binding to adherens junction protein, nectin-4. To disrupt spread, we introduced the point mutation H Y543A , a mutation previously described to inhibit nectin-4 binding, in the Ad-H vector. Co-transduction of Ad-F and Ad-H Y543A did not result in MeV-like infectious center formation. Finally, we assessed whether the MeV-related paramyxovirus Nipah (NiV) attachment and fusion proteins (G and F, respectively) support cell-to-cell spread. Co-transduction of HAE with Ad-NiV-G and Ad-NiV-F did not result in infectious center formation, suggesting that decoupling of the membrane fusion apparatus function from replication is a unique feature of the MeV envelope glycoproteins. IMPORTANCE Measles virus is a highly contagious pathogen. We characterized a mechanism by which measles virus spreads rapidly through the cells that line the human airway in an ex vivo model. We show that the proteins of the viral membrane fusion apparatus, hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F), move independently from and reach newly infected cells before the proteins of the replicative complex. Thus, viral protein spread is assembled and arranged in order (i.e., marshaled ). Using adenovirus-based vectors, we show that co-expression of H and F proteins promotes rapid sequential spread to multiple cells and the formation of infectious centers. Further elucidation of the mechanism of measles virus amplification and cell-to-cell spread within the lung may help explain its highly contagious nature.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 麻疹病毒(MeV)是传染性最强的人类呼吸道病原体。为了了解它如何在气道中传播,我们感染了分化良好的人气道上皮细胞(HAE)的原代培养物。我们发现 MeV 附着蛋白(血凝素,H)、融合蛋白(F)和组装组织蛋白(基质,M)先于复制复合体蛋白到达新感染的细胞,并且独立于复制复合体蛋白。为了表征 MeV 传播的机制,我们生成了复制缺陷型腺病毒 媒介,它以多西环素诱导的方式表达 MeV M、F 和 H 蛋白。这种病毒 媒介 形成了感染中心,保留了与 MeV 感染类似的上皮功能。为了进一步剖析这个过程,我们生成了表达单个 MeV 蛋白的 Ad 媒介,称为 Ad-M、Ad-F 和 Ad-H。用单、双和三 Ad 媒介 组合转导 HAE 表明,Ad-F 和 Ad-H 对于形成 MeV 样感染中心是必要且充分的。MeV 通过 H 蛋白与粘附连接蛋白 nectin-4 结合进入气道上皮并在气道上皮内传播。为了破坏传播,我们在 Ad-H 媒介 中引入了点 突变 H Y543A,这是先前描述的抑制 nectin-4 结合的 突变。Ad-F和Ad-H Y543A的共转导没有导致MeV样感染中心的形成。最后,我们评估了 MeV 相关副粘病毒尼帕 (NiV) 附着蛋白和融合蛋白(分别为 G 和 F)是否支持细胞间传播。HAE 与 Ad-NiV-G 和 Ad-NiV-F 的共转导不会导致感染中心的形成,这表明膜融合装置功能与复制的解偶联是 MeV 包膜糖蛋白的独特特征。重要性 麻疹病毒是一种高度传染性的病原体。我们在离体模型中描述了麻疹病毒通过人体呼吸道内壁细胞快速传播的机制。我们表明,病毒膜融合装置的蛋白质,血凝素(H)和融合蛋白(F),独立于复制复合物的蛋白质移动并先到达新感染的细胞。因此,病毒蛋白传播按顺序组装和排列(即编组)。使用基于腺病毒的 媒介,我们发现 H 和 F 蛋白的共表达促进快速顺序传播到多个细胞和感染中心的形成。进一步阐明麻疹病毒在肺部扩增和细胞间传播的机制可能有助于解释其高度传染性。

papers.title: Effect of bacteriophages on cytokine production by human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and their subpopulations
papers.abstract: Introduction Fulfilling a vision that extends beyond their role as antibiotic alternatives, bacteriophages are now recognized as active immunomodulators, a concept aligning with early hypotheses of their biological activity. In addition to their bactericidal action, these properties require detailed investigation. This study aims to characterize the immunomodulatory effects of bacteriophages on pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine production by human immune cells isolated from healthy blood donors. Methods We assessed the secretion of a comprehensive panel of 11 cytokines (including IFN-γ, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10) by peripheral blood mononuclear cells and their isolated subpopulations (B and T lymphocytes, helper and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and monocytes). The cells were incubated for 24 hours with purified Escherichia coli phage T4 and therapeutic staphylococcal phage A5/80. Reference cells were incubated with lipopolysaccharide from E. coli B at a concentration corresponding to its activity in the applied phage preparations. For comparison, we also assessed cytokine responses to human adenovirus 5, used as a benchmark for a virus capable of infecting human cells. Results Cell-specific analysis revealed a distinct hierarchy in immune responsiveness: our data suggest that monocytes may act as the primary sensors driving cytokine signatures, while we did not confirm a discernible direct response in B, natural killer, and cytotoxic T cells. Importantly, the magnitude of these responses was markedly lower than the robust inflammatory cytokine secretion triggered by human adenovirus 5, providing context for the phage-induced effects relative to a viral infection of human cells and underscoring the limited inflammatory footprint of therapeutic phages. Conclusion These results improve our understanding of phage–human immune system interactions, which is important for appreciating their broader impact on human homeostasis and for assessing the safety of phage therapy.

papers.title_zh: 噬菌体对人外周血单个核细胞及其亚群产生细胞因子的影响
papers.source_body_en: Introduction Fulfilling a vision that extends beyond their role as antibiotic alternatives, bacteriophages are now recognized as active immunomodulators, a concept aligning with early hypotheses of their biological activity. In addition to their bactericidal action, these properties require detailed investigation. This study aims to characterize the immunomodulatory effects of bacteriophages on pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine production by human immune cells isolated from healthy blood donors. Methods We assessed the secretion of a comprehensive panel of 11 cytokines (including IFN-γ, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10) by peripheral blood mononuclear cells and their isolated subpopulations (B and T lymphocytes, helper and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and monocytes). The cells were incubated for 24 hours with purified Escherichia coli phage T4 and therapeutic staphylococcal phage A5/80. Reference cells were incubated with lipopolysaccharide from E. coli B at a concentration corresponding to its activity in the applied phage preparations. For comparison, we also assessed cytokine responses to human adenovirus 5, used as a benchmark for a virus capable of infecting human cells. Results Cell-specific analysis revealed a distinct hierarchy in immune responsiveness: our data suggest that monocytes may act as the primary sensors driving cytokine signatures, while we did not confirm a discernible direct response in B, natural killer, and cytotoxic T cells. Importantly, the magnitude of these responses was markedly lower than the robust inflammatory cytokine secretion triggered by human adenovirus 5, providing context for the phage-induced effects relative to a viral infection of human cells and underscoring the limited inflammatory footprint of therapeutic phages. Conclusion These results improve our understanding of phage–human immune system interactions, which is important for appreciating their broader impact on human homeostasis and for assessing the safety of phage therapy.
papers.abstract_zh: 简介 噬菌体实现了超越其作为抗生素替代品的作用的愿景,现在被认为是主动免疫调节剂,这一概念与其生物活性的早期假设相一致。除了杀菌作用外,这些特性还需要详细研究。本研究旨在表征噬菌体对从健康献血者中分离出的人类免疫细胞产生促炎和抗炎细胞因子的免疫调节作用。方法 我们评估了外周血单核细胞及其分离亚群(B 和 T 淋巴细胞、辅助和细胞毒性 T 淋巴细胞、自然杀伤细胞和单核细胞)对 11 种细胞因子(包括 IFN-γ、IL-6、TNF-α 和 IL-10)的综合分泌。将细胞与纯化的大肠杆菌噬菌体 T4 和治疗性葡萄球菌噬菌体 A5/80 一起孵育 24 小时。将参考细胞与来自大肠杆菌 B 的脂多糖一起孵育,其浓度与其在所应用的噬菌体制剂中的活性相对应。为了进行比较,我们还评估了对 人腺病毒 5 的细胞因子反应,用作能够感染人类细胞的病毒的基准。结果细胞特异性分析揭示了免疫反应的明显层次结构:我们的数据表明单核细胞可能充当驱动细胞因子特征的主要传感器,而我们没有证实 B 细胞、自然杀伤细胞和细胞毒性 T 细胞中存在可辨别的直接反应。重要的是,这些反应的强度明显低于 人腺病毒 5 触发的强烈炎症细胞因子分泌,为噬菌体诱导的与人类细胞病毒感染相关的效应提供了背景,并强调了治疗性噬菌体的有限炎症足迹。结论这些结果提高了我们对噬菌体与人类免疫系统相互作用的理解,这对于了解它们对人类体内平衡的更广泛影响和评估噬菌体治疗的安全性非常重要。

papers.title: Respiratory Viruses in the Air of Shared Indoor Environments: Multi-Country Molecular Surveillance Across Europe (TwinAIR)
papers.abstract: Indoor environments are the dominant setting for human exposure to respiratory viruses, yet routine molecular surveillance of indoor air remains rare outside single-site studies. Within the Horizon Europe TwinAIR project, a single harmonised workflow was applied to 102 indoor air samples (2000 L each) collected between October 2024 and February 2026 at ten pilot settings in Germany, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain, Greece and Sweden, covering university teaching rooms, school classrooms and staff rooms, healthcare-associated offices, workplace offices, an elderly care facility and public transport vehicles. Air was collected onto gelatine membrane filters with a Sartorius MD8 Airport sampler, total nucleic acid was extracted with the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit, and five targets—SARS-CoV-2, human adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus A/B, influenza A and rhinovirus—were quantified against target-specific standard curves as genome copies per cubic metre (GC/m3). At least one target was detected in 84 of 102 samples (82.4%; 95% CI 73.8–88.5). SARS-CoV-2 was the most frequent and most abundant target (64.7%; up to 8.36 × 106 GC/m3) and adenovirus was the second most frequent though consistently low in concentration (33.3%); both were recovered from all six countries. Rhinovirus (14.7%, five countries), RSV A/B (8.8%, four) and influenza A (6.9%, four) were detected less often yet reached high concentrations when present, showing that detection frequency alone substantially understates airborne viral burden. Detection of viral genome does not establish infectivity.

papers.source_body_en: Indoor environments are the dominant setting for human exposure to respiratory viruses, yet routine molecular surveillance of indoor air remains rare outside single-site studies. Within the Horizon Europe TwinAIR project, a single harmonised workflow was applied to 102 indoor air samples (2000 L each) collected between October 2024 and February 2026 at ten pilot settings in Germany, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain, Greece and Sweden, covering university teaching rooms, school classrooms and staff rooms, healthcare-associated offices, workplace offices, an elderly care facility and public transport vehicles. Air was collected onto gelatine membrane filters with a Sartorius MD8 Airport sampler, total nucleic acid was extracted with the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit, and five targets—SARS-CoV-2, human adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus A/B, influenza A and rhinovirus—were quantified against target-specific standard curves as genome copies per cubic metre (GC/m3). At least one target was detected in 84 of 102 samples (82.4%; 95% CI 73.8–88.5). SARS-CoV-2 was the most frequent and most abundant target (64.7%; up to 8.36 × 106 GC/m3) and adenovirus was the second most frequent though consistently low in concentration (33.3%); both were recovered from all six countries. Rhinovirus (14.7%, five countries), RSV A/B (8.8%, four) and influenza A (6.9%, four) were detected less often yet reached high concentrations when present, showing that detection frequency alone substantially understates airborne viral burden. Detection of viral genome does not establish infectivity.
papers.abstract_zh: 室内环境是人类接触呼吸道病毒的主要环境,但室内空气的常规分子 监测 在单点研究之外仍然很少见。在 Horizo​​n Europe TwinAIR 项目中,对 2024 年 10 月至 2026 年 2 月期间在德国、英国、爱尔兰、西班牙、希腊和瑞典的 10 个试点地点收集的 102 个室内空气样本(每个 2000 升)应用了单一协调工作流程,涵盖大学教学室、学校教室和教职员室、医疗保健相关办公室、工作场所办公室、老年护理设施和公共交通车辆。使用 Sartorius MD8 Airport 采样器将空气收集到明胶膜过滤器上,使用 QIAamp Viral RNA Mini 试剂盒提取总核酸,并根据目标特异性标准曲线对五个目标(SARS-CoV-2、人腺病毒、呼吸道合胞病毒 A/B、甲型流感和鼻病毒)进行定量,即每立方米 基因组 拷贝数 (GC/m3)。102 个样本中的 84 个样本中至少检测到一个目标(82.4%;95% CI 73.8–88.5)。SARS-CoV-2 是最常见和最丰富的目标(64.7%;高达 8.36 × 106 GC/m3),腺病毒是第二常见的目标,但浓度始终较低(33.3%);两者均已从所有六个国家找到。鼻病毒(14.7%,五个国家)、RSV A/B(8.8%,四个)和甲型流感病毒(6.9%,四个)的检测频率较低,但在存在时仍达到高浓度,表明仅检测频率就大大低估了空气传播的病毒负荷。检测到病毒 基因组 并不能确定其传染性。

papers.full_text: AbstractBackground: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) remain a major cause of hospitalization and mortality, particularly among children and other vulnerable populations. Early identification of pathogens and disease severity is essential for clinical decision-making. This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort.Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival. ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. ViVI scores reflect clinical severity at presentation, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity. Coinfections include viral-viral and viral-bacterial combinations detected by multiplex PCR and/or standard microbiological methods.HRSV: human respiratory syncytial virus; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ViVI Score: ViVI Disease Severity ScoreOrganism / CoinfectionMedian ViVI scoreIQR (interquartile range)Number of patientsType of infectionHuman respiratory syncytial viruses A/B20.513.538Single InfectionStaphylococcus aureus20195Single InfectionInfluenza B virus20.510.254Single InfectionStreptococcus pneumoniae296.53Single InfectionHuman rhinovirus3562Single InfectionHuman adenovirus3701Single InfectionHuman parainfluenza virus 44201Single InfectionHRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2113.7510CoinfectionHRSV + Human rhinovirus2043CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B virus32162CoinfectionHRSV + Staphylococcus aureus 2032CoinfectionAdenovirus + HRSV1601CoinfectionCoronavirus OC43 + HRSV1601CoinfectionMetapneumovirus + HRSV4501CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 3 + Parainfluenza virus 41101CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 4 + Parechovirus801CoinfectionRhinovirus + Staphylococcus aureus 2901CoinfectionInfluenza B virus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2901CoinfectionStaphylococcus aureus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 3501CoinfectionHRSV + Parainfluenza virus 41501CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B + Staphylococcus aureus 2701CoinfectionClinical outcomes and mortalityThe overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases.Predictive utility of the ViVI ScoreA total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3).Figure 3Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating the predictive performance of the ViVI Disease Severity Score for mortalityThe ROC plot displays the relationship between the false positive fraction (FPF: 1 − specificity) on the x-axis and the true positive fraction (TPF: sensitivity) on the y-axis across decision thresholds. The blue curve with red markers represents the binormal ROC curve fitted using maximum-likelihood estimation (JROCFIT), while the grey envelopes depict the 95% confidence interval around the fitted curve. The empirical (nonparametric) ROC operating points are shown as black markers (with the green connection, where applicable). Overall discrimination was excellent (fitted AUC ≈ 0.946; empirical AUC ≈ 0.942), with the curve lying close to the upper-left corner, indicating high sensitivity at low false-positive rates.The ROC curve lies close to the upper-left corner, indicating excellent discriminatory performance of the ViVI Score for predicting mortality across a range of decision thresholds (Figure 3). Using the ViVI Score as a mortality predictor and classifying death as the event, a low cutoff of ViVI ≥15 yielded 100% sensitivity for death (24/24) but low specificity (29.0%, 27/93) (TP=24, FN=0, TN=27, FP=66). In contrast, a high cutoff of ViVI ≥45 yielded 100% specificity (93/93) but low sensitivity (25.0%, 6/24) (TP=6, FN=18, TN=93, FP=0). The optimal threshold by Youden's J was ViVI ≥30, which provided balanced performance (sensitivity 83.3% (20/24) and specificity 91.4% (85/93); overall accuracy 89.7% (105/117)) (TP=20, FN=4, TN=85, FP=8). Patients with ViVI ≥30 had markedly increased odds of death compared with those with ViVI <30 (odds ratio 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; Fisher's exact test p=1.4 × 10−12). DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival.
full_text_sections.results: ResultsA total of 117 patients were included in the study. The cohort was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults. The median age of the study population was 2.0 years (IQR 0.5-7.5 years). The male-to-female ratio was 1.81:1, indicating a male predominance.Pathogen detection profile from the multiplex PCROut of the 117 patients, 81 (69.2%) were positive for at least one respiratory pathogen using multiplex PCR. Multiplex respiratory pathogen testing identified HRSV A/B as the most frequently detected pathogen (n=60), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=16), Staphylococcus aureus (n=11), human rhinovirus (n=8), and influenza B virus (n=7). Lower detection rates were observed for human parainfluenza virus type 4 (n=3), human adenovirus (n=2), human coronavirus OC43, human metapneumovirus A/B, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and human parechovirus (each n=1). No cases were detected for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, human bocavirus, human coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, and NL63, human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2, influenza A virus (including H1N1), or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Conversely, 36 patients tested negative for all pathogens, indicating either non-infectious etiologies or undetected organisms outside the panel’s scope (Figure 2). Additionally, six cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) due to HRSV were documented in a subset of adult patients, along with HRSV positivity among 13 children with underlying hematological disorders.Figure 2Distribution of pathogen positivity by multiplex PCR in patient samplesHRSV A/B was the most frequently identified organism, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Rhinovirus.mPCR+: multiplex polymerase chain reaction positive for at least one pathogen; RSV A/B: respiratory syncytial virus types A and B; S. pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae; S. aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; HRV: human rhinovirus; IBV: influenza B virus; HPIV-4: human parainfluenza virus type 4; HAdV: human adenovirus; HCoV-OC43: human coronavirus OC43; HMPV A/B: human metapneumovirus types A and B; HPIV-3: human parainfluenza virus type 3; HPeV: human parechovirus; NPD: no pathogen detected; ARDS: acute respiratory distress syndrome; HD: hematological disordersPathogen detection profile from conventional culturesBlood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%); five were adults, and 35 were children. Among the positive blood cultures, 18 yielded methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, seven Escherichia coli, seven Klebsiella pneumoniae, seven Streptococcus pneumoniae, and one yielded both S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Lower respiratory tract aerobic cultures were positive in 48 patients (five adults and 43 children), yielding S. pneumoniae in 15, E. coli in 12, confluent growth of K. pneumoniae in 10, and S. aureus in 10; one patient had both S. pneumoniae and S. aureus.Biomarker profileElevated PCT (>0.5 ng/mL) was observed in 55/117 patients (47.0%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Markedly elevated CRP (>10 mg/dL) was observed in 101/117 patients (86.3%), including all 40 patients with positive blood cultures. Positive D-dimer, suggestive of a hypercoagulable state, was observed in 35 patients, of whom 30 had sepsis.ViVI Score distributionThe median ViVI Score across all patients was 22. Distribution of ViVI scores varied based on pathogen and infection type. Among single infections, HRSV A/B was most frequent (n=38) with a median ViVI score of 20.5 (IQR 13.5). Other single pathogens were less common, including Staphylococcus aureus (n=5; median 20 (IQR 19)), Influenza B (n=4; median 20.5 (IQR 10.25)), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=3; median 29 (IQR 6.5)), Human rhinovirus (n=2; median 35 (IQR 6)), and individual cases of adenovirus (median 37) and parainfluenza virus 4 (median 42). Among coinfections, HRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common (n=10; median 21 (IQR 13.75)). Other HRSV coinfections included HRSV + rhinovirus (n=3; median 20 (IQR 4)), HRSV + Influenza B (n=2; median 32 (IQR 16)), and HRSV + Staphylococcus aureus (n=2; median 20 (IQR 3)), while the remaining coinfections occurred as single cases with variable ViVI scores (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of median ViVI Scores across respiratory pathogens and coinfectionsThe table summarizes the median ViVI score with the corresponding interquartile range (IQR) for each identified organism or organism combination, along with the number of affected patients and classification as single infection or coinfection. ViVI scores reflect clinical severity at presentation, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity. Coinfections include viral-viral and viral-bacterial combinations detected by multiplex PCR and/or standard microbiological methods.HRSV: human respiratory syncytial virus; PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ViVI Score: ViVI Disease Severity ScoreOrganism / CoinfectionMedian ViVI scoreIQR (interquartile range)Number of patientsType of infectionHuman respiratory syncytial viruses A/B20.513.538Single InfectionStaphylococcus aureus20195Single InfectionInfluenza B virus20.510.254Single InfectionStreptococcus pneumoniae296.53Single InfectionHuman rhinovirus3562Single InfectionHuman adenovirus3701Single InfectionHuman parainfluenza virus 44201Single InfectionHRSV + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2113.7510CoinfectionHRSV + Human rhinovirus2043CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B virus32162CoinfectionHRSV + Staphylococcus aureus 2032CoinfectionAdenovirus + HRSV1601CoinfectionCoronavirus OC43 + HRSV1601CoinfectionMetapneumovirus + HRSV4501CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 3 + Parainfluenza virus 41101CoinfectionParainfluenza virus 4 + Parechovirus801CoinfectionRhinovirus + Staphylococcus aureus 2901CoinfectionInfluenza B virus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 2901CoinfectionStaphylococcus aureus + Streptococcus pneumoniae 3501CoinfectionHRSV + Parainfluenza virus 41501CoinfectionHRSV + Influenza B + Staphylococcus aureus 2701CoinfectionClinical outcomes and mortalityThe overall mortality rate in the cohort was 20.5% (24/117). Of particular concern was the subgroup of patients presenting with SARI and culture-confirmed sepsis (n=40), in which mortality rose dramatically to 60% (24/40). This suggests that progression to sepsis remains the strongest indicator of poor outcomes in SARI cases.Predictive utility of the ViVI ScoreA total of 117 cases were analyzed (93 survivors and 24 deaths). ROC analysis using JROCFIT demonstrated excellent discrimination between survivors and non-survivors (fitted AUC 0.946 (SD 0.022); empiric AUC 0.942) (Figure 3).Figure 3Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrating the predictive performance of the ViVI Disease Severity Score for mortalityThe ROC plot displays the relationship between the false positive fraction (FPF: 1 − specificity) on the x-axis and the true positive fraction (TPF: sensitivity) on the y-axis across decision thresholds.
