full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. The global burden of HRSV is substantial. A systematic analysis estimated 33.0 million HRSV-associated acute lower respiratory infection episodes, 3.6 million hospital admissions, and 101,400 deaths among children younger than five years in 2019, with the majority of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries [19].The frequency of co-infections observed in our cohort is also consistent with previous pediatric SARI studies using multiplex molecular platforms. Lamrani Hanchi et al. reported pathogen detection in 72.5% of hospitalized children and co-infection in 23.3%, highlighting the ability of multiplex PCR to identify multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen [20]. Similarly, studies incorporating digital surveillance and virological characterization have emphasized the value of combining pathogen detection with standardized clinical information [21,22]. These findings support the use of syndromic molecular testing as an adjunct to conventional microbiological investigations in patients with severe respiratory disease. However, detection of a respiratory pathogen does not necessarily establish causality, particularly for respiratory viruses that may be detected during prolonged shedding or asymptomatic infection. Therefore, multiplex PCR results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, disease severity, and conventional microbiological results.The exceptionally high mortality observed among SARI patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) was substantially higher than the overall mortality in the cohort. This finding is consistent with pediatric intensive-care data demonstrating significant mortality among children with bloodstream-infection-associated severe sepsis [23]. The finding emphasizes the importance of early recognition of bacterial superinfection and sepsis among patients presenting with severe respiratory illness, particularly when clinical deterioration or evidence of systemic infection is present.HRSV-associated disease severity is influenced by age and underlying clinical conditions. Recent multicenter pediatric data have demonstrated increased risk of severe RSV disease among younger children, premature infants, and older children with pulmonary or neurological, neuromuscular, or developmental conditions [24]. In our cohort, children with underlying hematological disorders represented an important high-risk subgroup, and HRSV-associated ARDS was associated with severe clinical outcomes. These findings reinforce the importance of identifying underlying risk factors when assessing patients with HRSV-associated SARI.The ViVI Score provided a structured approach to clinical severity assessment. Previous work has emphasized the importance of standardized severity assessment for respiratory viral illness and SARI [5]. More recent severity scales have also been evaluated to support respiratory hospitalization surveillance and viral genomic surveillance [25]. In our cohort, a ViVI score of ≥30 demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with an AUC of 0.946. This finding supports the potential utility of standardized severity assessment for identifying patients at increased risk of poor outcomes. However, prospective validation in independent populations is required before this threshold can be considered for broader clinical implementation.Raised PCT and CRP concentrations were associated with culture-positive sepsis and adverse clinical outcomes in our cohort. Previous pediatric data have evaluated PCT and CRP as markers of sepsis, with PCT potentially providing useful information regarding bacterial infection and disease severity [26]. However, neither biomarker should be interpreted as a stand-alone diagnostic test. Their value is greatest when interpreted together with the clinical presentation, microbiological findings, and other laboratory parameters.The findings also have implications for respiratory disease surveillance and clinical triage. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment can provide information on both pathogen circulation and clinical severity [21,22,25]. Such an approach may be particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings, where molecular diagnostic capacity is concentrated at tertiary-care facilities, and timely referral of patients with severe disease remains important. In primary-care settings, recognition of clinical warning signs and timely referral remain essential, while tertiary-care molecular testing can provide additional etiological information.The post-pandemic period is particularly relevant for respiratory pathogen surveillance because changes in population immunity, non-pharmaceutical interventions, and patterns of viral circulation may influence the timing and intensity of respiratory virus activity [16]. Continued surveillance is therefore important for identifying changing epidemiological patterns, detecting populations at increased risk of severe disease, and informing healthcare preparedness.The predominance of HRSV in our cohort also highlights the importance of preventive strategies. Current approaches to prevention of severe RSV disease include maternal vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibody strategies, particularly for infants at greatest risk of severe disease [27]. Continued pathogen-specific surveillance will be important for evaluating the epidemiological impact of these interventions.The study has several strengths. It integrates multiplex molecular diagnostics with conventional microbiological culture, inflammatory biomarkers, and standardized severity assessment, allowing simultaneous evaluation of pathogen distribution, bacterial superinfection, disease severity, and mortality. The use of a standardized severity score also enabled quantitative assessment of the relationship between clinical severity and mortality.In this study, several limitations should nevertheless be considered. The retrospective single-center design and relatively small sample size limit generalizability. The cohort was predominantly pediatric (103 children and 14 adults), which reflects the population evaluated at our center during the study period. Consequently, the findings, particularly those related to pathogen distribution, disease severity, and mortality risk stratification, should be interpreted primarily in the context of pediatric SARI and may not be directly generalizable to adult SARI populations. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsHRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen identified among hospitalized patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI. Multiplex molecular testing provided useful etiological information, while the ViVI Score demonstrated good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort. Further prospective studies in larger and more diverse populations are needed to validate these findings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSevere acute respiratory infections (SARI) pose a significant global health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines SARI as an acute respiratory illness with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization [1]. However, this syndromic definition does not provide information regarding the underlying etiological agent or the individual risk of adverse outcomes. SARI may result from a wide range of viral and bacterial pathogens, and conventional diagnostic methods may not always provide a timely or comprehensive etiological diagnosis.Before the COVID-19 pandemic, SARI detection was largely syndromic, relying on clinical presentation and limited diagnostic capacity [2]. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for strengthening surveillance systems and pathogen identification. In India, surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases is supported through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, including laboratory-based and information technology-enabled surveillance [3].SARI constitutes a major cause of healthcare utilization and hospitalization and may require referral to secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, particularly among young children, older adults, and individuals with underlying comorbidities. Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2].In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4].To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison.The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7].Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings. papers.title_original: Molecular Etiology and Mortality Risk Stratification of Non-SARS-CoV-2 Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in a Predominantly Pediatric Cohort: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the molecular etiology of severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) in a pediatric cohort, excluding SARS-CoV-2, to better understand the role of other pathogens in causing severe respiratory disease.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective observational study analyzed data from patients admitted with SARI during September to December 2021 at a tertiary care hospital in North India. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults, with inclusion criteria based on the WHO SARI case definition.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured, and mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
analysis.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the most frequently identified pathogen. Blood cultures were positive in 34.2% of patients, predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, rising to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the significant role of HRSV A/B in causing severe respiratory infections in children, with the ViVI Score showing good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings contribute to understanding the etiology of SARI in pediatric populations and emphasize the importance of HRSV in severe respiratory disease, informing targeted surveillance and management strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for missing pathogens outside the tested panel. The evidence is moderate due to the reliance on existing data and the absence of prospective validation.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective study investigated the molecular etiology of severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) in a pediatric cohort in North India, excluding SARS-CoV-2. It analyzed data from 117 patients admitted between September and December 2021, using multiplex PCR and microbiological cultures. The main results showed that 69.2% of patients tested positive for at least one respiratory pathogen, with HRSV A/B being the most common. Blood cultures were positive in 34.2% of patients, primarily identifying methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% in patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. The study interprets these findings as highlighting the significant role of HRSV in pediatric SARI and the utility of the ViVI Score in predicting mortality. The results suggest that HRSV is an important cause of severe respiratory illness in children, supporting targeted surveillance and management. However, the study's retrospective design and potential for missing pathogens limit the confidence in its findings, resulting in a moderate evidence assessment.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the molecular etiology of severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) in a pediatric cohort, excluding SARS-CoV-2, to better understand the role of other pathogens in causing severe respiratory disease.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: This retrospective observational study analyzed data from patients admitted with SARI during September to December 2021 at a tertiary care hospital in North India. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults, with inclusion criteria based on the WHO SARI case definition.
elements_en.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured, and mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
elements_en.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the most frequently identified pathogen. Blood cultures were positive in 34.2% of patients, predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, rising to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the significant role of HRSV A/B in causing severe respiratory infections in children, with the ViVI Score showing good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings contribute to understanding the etiology of SARI in pediatric populations and emphasize the importance of HRSV in severe respiratory disease, informing targeted surveillance and management strategies.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for missing pathogens outside the tested panel. The evidence is moderate due to the reliance on existing data and the absence of prospective validation.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查儿童 队列研究 严重急性呼吸道感染 (SARI) 的分子病因学(不包括 SARS-CoV-2),以更好地了解其他病原体在引起严重呼吸道疾病中的作用。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性观察研究分析了 2021 年 9 月至 12 月在印度北部一家三级护理医院收治的 SARI 患者的数据。研究人群主要是儿科,包括 103 名儿童和 14 名成人,纳入标准基于 WHO SARI 病例定义。
elements_zh.methods: 使用多重聚合酶链反应(PCR)以及血液和下呼吸道培养物来鉴定呼吸道病原体。测量血清 C 反应蛋白 (CRP)、降钙素原 (PCT) 和 D-二聚体,并使用 ViVI 评分和受试者工作特征 (ROC) 曲线分析评估 死亡率 预测。
elements_zh.main_results: 多重 PCR 在 69.2% 的患者中检测到至少一种呼吸道病原体,其中 HRSV A/B 是最常见的病原体。34.2% 的患者血培养呈阳性,主要为甲氧西林敏感金黄色葡萄球菌。总体 死亡率 为 20.5%,在培养确诊的败血症患者中上升至 60%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 该研究强调了 HRSV A/B 在引起儿童严重呼吸道感染中的重要作用,ViVI 评分在该 队列研究 中显示出对 死亡率 风险的良好辨别能力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现有助于了解儿科人群中 SARI 的病因,并强调 HRSV 在严重呼吸道疾病中的重要性,为有针对性的 监测 和管理策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计和测试组之外可能缺失的病原体而受到限制。由于依赖现有数据且缺乏前瞻性验证,证据是中等的。

papers.title_zh: 以儿科为主的非 SARS-CoV-2 严重急性呼吸道感染的分子病因学和 死亡率 风险分层 队列研究:印度北部一家三级护理医院的回顾性研究
papers.source_body_en: This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort.Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. papers.title: Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities

source_records.title: Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities
Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: While certain forms of lymphoma—such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma—are classified as curable, with over half of all patients achieving remission following first-line therapy, a significant proportion of patients still suffer from relapsed or refractory disease. Through autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can significantly improve survival rates, their widespread clinical utility is constrained by logistical bottlenecks, manufacturing complexities, and high financial burdens. Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies have achieved striking success against hematologic malignancies, but their clinical adoption is often hindered by the requirement for continuous infusion. Consequently, systemically delivered oncolytic viruses engineered to express immunotherapeutic elements have emerged as highly innovative alternatives. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and outlines the therapeutic potential of oncolytic virotherapy in the fight against hematopoietic malignancies. We cross-examined a robust dataset of over 100 preclinical investigations to critically assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of more than ten diverse oncolytic virus platforms developed for blood cancer treatment, alongside multiple early-phase clinical trials that are completed or currently underway. By synthesizing these preclinical and clinical data, we propose three critical development pathways—enhancing target specificity, arming viral vectors, and designing synergistic combination regimens—to accelerate the translation of clinically viable oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology. Introduction and methodologyOncolytic viruses (OVs) have been widely studied in solid tumors, typically through intratumoral administration. In contrast, hematopoietic malignancies—which inherently require systemic drug delivery rather than local injection—have historically received less attention as primary targets for OV therapy. In this review, we explored data from clinical applications and trials, tracing evidence back through preclinical and basic research. By analyzing the current landscape of utilizing OVs to treat hematopoietic malignancies, we highlight this systemic targeting paradigm as possessing a uniquely favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.This mini-review was conducted by searching the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026 using the terms “oncolytic virus” and “hematopoietic malignancies” or “blood cancer” or “lymphoma” or “leukemia” or “multiple myeloma.” Additional references were identified through citation tracking of relevant reviews and primary studies, prioritizing the most recent and clinically significant trials, preclinical advances, and mechanistic insights.Inclusion criteria: Studies were included if they evaluated live oncolytic virus platforms specifically targeting hematopoietic malignancies, lymphomas, leukemias, or multiple myeloma in preclinical models or clinical trials. Only articles published in English were considered, with no restrictions applied to publication date or study type.Exclusion criteria: Non-English articles, abstract-only publications lacking primary data, and studies focusing strictly on solid tumors without hematological evaluations were excluded.Initial database searches yielded a combined pool of records. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining articles were screened by the first reviewer based on title and abstract. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies regarding article selection or data extraction were resolved through consensus discussion between both reviewers prior to final inclusion Supplementary Tables and Figure 1. For each eligible study, information regarding study design, disease indication, efficacy-related outcomes, safety profiles, and adverse events associated with oncolytic virotherapy was collected and summarized.Figure 1Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers. Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers recorded in the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases in the past three decades are distributed according to the publication year (X-axis) and virus types (Y-axis). For preclinical studies, the numbers inside the blue circles indicate the number of studies conducted for each OV in that year; those without numbers indicate that only one study was conducted. The Pteropine orthoreovirus (Sikamat virus) grouped under ‘Other’ is a distinct bat-borne species and not the mammalian reovirus (pelareorep) shown as ‘Reovirus’. Detail information was collected in Supplementary Tables 1, 2, from which the figure was generated using Python (Matplotlib).Scatter plot showing years of publication for studies on various oncolytic viruses from 1995 to 2025. Blue circles represent pre-clinical studies, and red stars denote clinical studies or case reports. Each row corresponds to a different virus, including measles virus, adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, reovirus, vaccinia virus, myxoma virus, Newcastle disease virus, herpes simplex virus, and others. Most clinical studies occur after 2015, with recent entries for SARS-CoV-2. A legend specifies the meaning of symbols. The start: clinical case reports of tumor regressions after virus infectionThe therapeutic potential of viruses in oncology was initially inferred from clinical observations of spontaneous tumor regression following naturally acquired viral infections. Notably, transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma were historically reported during concurrent influenza or measles virus (MV) infections. More recently, similar remissions have been documented in hematologic malignancies following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. The inherent tumor-selectivity demonstrated by many wild-type viruses is largely attributed to the altered cellular landscape of neoplastic cells. Specifically, the hallmarks of cancer create a permissive microenvironment that overlaps significantly with cellular features required for efficient viral replication. Oncolytic viruses: a new generation of live cancer cell killersOVs are replication-competent, biologically active agents that exert anti-cancer effects through two principal mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis and indirect stimulation of systemic anti-tumor immunity. In hematologic malignancies, where cancer cells reside in immune-privileged niches such as the bone marrow or peripheral blood, this dual functionality is particularly advantageous. On one hand, OVs themselves exploit molecular vulnerabilities in malignant cells; on the other hand, OVs can be armed with immunomodulatory transgenes to amplify their therapeutic impact. Pre-clinical studies on evaluating therapeutic OVs in blood cancersTo comprehensively examine and summarize the existing literature regarding OVs in blood cancer therapy and explore treatment-related outcomes, we first retrieved citations using the terms indicated in the Methodology section. After the title and abstract screening phase, the non-overlapping research articles were combined and analyzed. Then we grouped these studies according to the different virus types. Among them, MV was the most frequently studied in publications, followed by adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and reovirus (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Below, we will analyze the study setup and major outcomes of these studies based on different OV types.Although adenovirus was the most frequently applied one in clinical trials,1 only a handful of studies were performed in blood cancer treatment. These studies ranged from systematic evaluation to rational design of human adenoviruses for enhanced blood cancer therapy. In an earlier study by Qian and colleagues, E1B55K-deleted adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) armed with melanoma differentiation-associated gene-7/interleukin-24 (MDA-7/IL-24) was tested in a range of blood cancer cell lines. Although a potent anti-cancer effect was observed in vitro and in vivo, the effect was limited to Ad5 major receptor (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor)-expressing hematological malignancies (Qian et al., 2008). Follow-up studies solved the problem by using chimeric Ad35 fiber (Wang et al., 2009; Wenthe et al., 2020). Another study compared the growth-inhibition effect of adenovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV) on several cell lines; HSV was more effective (Zhang et al., 2011). Realizing the limitation from Ad5, a broad range of human adenoviruses were evaluated by Barry’s research group. They observed robust killing and delayed lymphoma growth by species D adenoviruses (Chen et al., 2011). However, in mouse B cell lymphoma model A20, only prophylactic immunization by adenovirus against A20 tumors can protect against A20 lymphomas; established A20 tumors were not controlled by A20-expressing adenovirus immunization (Weaver et al., 2011). While OV alone is not enough to control blood malignancies, a combination approach highlights the optimized development strategy. A rationally designed OAd5F35, Ad5-based chimeric virus with Ad35 fiber, armed with TMZ-CD40L and 4-1BBL was evaluated in combination with CAR-T therapy. The fiber switch to Ad35 enabled the use of CD46, which is up-regulated in hematological malignancies, thereby enhancing targeting and replication. Interestingly, OAd5F35 infection induced transgene expression and a change in immune markers. In combination with CAR-T therapy, the infected lymphoma cells were found to secrete chemokines to attract CAR-T cells, thereby increased CAR-T cell activation was observed. Importantly, the enhanced lymphoma cell killing was also observed in vivo in xenograft models (Wenthe et al., 2021). Similarly, a CD47 antibody expressing adenovirus (Ad5-hTert-E1A-IRES-E1B with mCMV-mCD47nb-Fc) as in situ tumor vaccination also showed positive immune-regulation and protection from tumor re-challenge (Zhang et al., 2022). These data suggested that adenovirus alone is not enough to control such aggressive hematological malignancies; a combination approach should be the development strategy of choice.Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), based on HSV-1, is so far the only OV approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of melanoma (Zhang T. et al., 2023). However, only a few studies have explored its potential in hematological malignancies. In the search for molecular indicators for permissiveness to HSV therapy, transcription factors downstream of Ras were evaluated in non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) cell lines infected with R3616, an HSV-1 with a deletion of the viral γ134.5 gene. Ras signaling was assessed by immunoblotting for different downstream effectors, which revealed ERK/ELK as a suitable predictive indicator for selection of cancer cells with increased sensitivity to HSV-based therapy (Esfandyari et al., 2009). As G47Δ was approved in Japan in 2021 (Frampton, 2022), a similar version of this OV was evaluated in a broad panel of 26 cell lines and 15 primary cells derived from various lineages of hematological malignancies (Ishino et al., 2021). The expression of an HSV-1 receptor, nectin-1, was identified as a determining factor in the oncolytic effect determined by viral entry and cytotoxicity. Although only a low level of virus replication was detected in hematological cancer cells, the virus could induce immunogenic cell death and kill the malignant cells. Importantly, this study demonstrated that systemic tumor-specific CD8 + T cell responses efficiently concentrated at tumor sites, suggesting that local intratumoral injection of HSV-1 is expected to provoke effective immune responses even for systemic tumors such as hematological malignancies. Recently, an oncolytic type II HSV (oHSV2) was explored in the treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (Zhang J. et al., 2023). In comparison with the clinical chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin (DOX), oHSV2 revealed a better therapeutic profile on the apoptotic, invasive, and proliferative capacity of DLBCL cells in vitro. Moreover, oHSV2 can also inhibit transplanted tumor growth and accelerate CD4 + T and CD8 + T cell infiltration in mice, with an acceptable safety profile in the organs of tumor-bearing animals. To explore the potential of combination therapy with immune-checkpoint inhibitors, this study also showed oHSV2 can inhibit the PD-1/PD-L1 immune-checkpoint, thereby restraining cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) apoptosis and encouraging CTL proliferation. The combination therapy resulted in enhanced killing of malignant cells and inhibited tumor growth in mice. Similar to the adenovirus studies, combination therapy and the individual receptor profile are essential for further HSV application in hematological malignancies.The rat protoparvovirus H-1 (H-1PV) does not infect or cause any disease in humans, but has natural tropism for human cancer cells. H-1PV demonstrates a broad range of anticancer activities in several preclinical cancer models and in clinical trials (Geletneky et al., 2017; Bretscher and Marchini, 2019; Hajda et al., 2021). The first study to apply H-1PV to Burkitt’s lymphoma (BL)-derived cell lines showed high sensitivity to H-1PV-induced oncolysis in vitro. The H-1PV infection of BL lines is productive and leads to predominantly necrotic cell death. Importantly, normal B cells from healthy donors are resistant to H-1PV infection (Angelova et al., 2009). Then a large panel of lymphoma- and leukemia-derived cell lines was included to assess the capacity of H-1PV to target hematological malignancies. This study revealed that most cell lines are sensitive to H-1PV-induced cell death, and the progeny virion production, rather than virus entry, was the determining factor. Among all tested cells, DLBCL cells supported high levels of H-1PV progeny virion production and were almost totally eradicated by very low virus doses. Moreover, DLBCL cell lines with upregulated expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A1 conferring chemotherapy resistance were among the most sensitive H-1PV targets (Angelova et al., 2017). A recent study extended this work to cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). H-1PV infects and induces oncolysis in both classically grown CTCL suspension cultures and in a novel, in vivo-relevant, heterotypic spheroid model, but not in healthy donor controls, including peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). In CTCL spheroid co-cultures with PBMCs, treatment with the virus increased infiltration of the spheroids with immune cells (Angelova et al., 2024).Among oncolytic platforms, MV is the most extensively studied in hematological malignancies, owing to its vaccine safety record and its natural tropism for CD46 and the lymphocyte receptor SLAM/CD150 (Ong et al., 2006; Engeland and Ungerechts, 2021). Vaccine-strain MV was found to regress human B-cell lymphoma xenografts even in the presence of anti-MV antibodies (Grote et al., 2001). Subsequent improvement in specificity was achieved by retargeting viral entry. Vectors retargeted to CD20, armed with a prodrug convertase, and combined with cyclophosphamide and fludarabine regressed mantle cell lymphoma xenografts, though with limited survival benefit (Bucheit et al., 2003; Ungerechts et al., 2010). Analogous CD30 and CD38 retargeting extended the approach to Hodgkin lymphoma and myeloma (Peng et al., 2003; Hanauer et al., 2018). Importantly, efficacy was tracked with receptor usage and innate signaling. For instance, SLAM-dependent entry in mantle cell lymphoma virotherapy, EBV-driven CD150 upregulation and type I interferon responsiveness have been shown to determine susceptibility, and Bcl-2 has been shown to slow oncolysis in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Patel et al., 2011; Miest et al., 2013; Fernandez et al., 2014; Takeda et al., 2014). To facilitate systemic delivery in the face of anti-MV immunity, studies have shown that both carrier and mesenchymal stromal cells have the capacity to deliver the virus to sites of disseminated disease (Iankov et al., 2007; Castleton et al., 2014). In particular, the development of the thyroidal sodium iodide symporter-expressing MV-NIS has advanced MV into early-phase clinical testing for multiple myeloma (MM) (Dingli et al., 2004).Vaccinia virus (VV), a large-genome poxvirus that tolerates sizeable transgene insertions, has been used in blood cancers mainly as an arming and combination platform rather than as a bare oncolytic agent. An attenuated VV delivered by cytokine-induced killer cells trafficked to residual murine B-cell lymphoma and prevented relapse through acquired antitumor immunity (Contag et al., 2010). Its coding capacity has since carried both pro-apoptotic and immunomodulatory transgenes. Notably, immune-arming constructs have been developed to combine oncolysis with a defined effector mechanism. A CD19 bispecific T-cell engager recruited T cells, an anti-CD47 nanobody reprogrammed macrophages, and interleukin-18 relieved T-cell exhaustion, each prolonging survival in lymphoma models (Lei et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). The natural adjuvant embelin further enhanced replication and antitumor immunity (Wang et al., 2020). full_text_sections.abstract: While certain forms of lymphoma—such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma—are classified as curable, with over half of all patients achieving remission following first-line therapy, a significant proportion of patients still suffer from relapsed or refractory disease. Through autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can significantly improve survival rates, their widespread clinical utility is constrained by logistical bottlenecks, manufacturing complexities, and high financial burdens. Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies have achieved striking success against hematologic malignancies, but their clinical adoption is often hindered by the requirement for continuous infusion. Consequently, systemically delivered oncolytic viruses engineered to express immunotherapeutic elements have emerged as highly innovative alternatives. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and outlines the therapeutic potential of oncolytic virotherapy in the fight against hematopoietic malignancies. We cross-examined a robust dataset of over 100 preclinical investigations to critically assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of more than ten diverse oncolytic virus platforms developed for blood cancer treatment, alongside multiple early-phase clinical trials that are completed or currently underway. By synthesizing these preclinical and clinical data, we propose three critical development pathways—enhancing target specificity, arming viral vectors, and designing synergistic combination regimens—to accelerate the translation of clinically viable oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology.
full_text_sections.methods: Introduction and methodologyOncolytic viruses (OVs) have been widely studied in solid tumors, typically through intratumoral administration. In contrast, hematopoietic malignancies—which inherently require systemic drug delivery rather than local injection—have historically received less attention as primary targets for OV therapy. In this review, we explored data from clinical applications and trials, tracing evidence back through preclinical and basic research. By analyzing the current landscape of utilizing OVs to treat hematopoietic malignancies, we highlight this systemic targeting paradigm as possessing a uniquely favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.This mini-review was conducted by searching the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026 using the terms “oncolytic virus” and “hematopoietic malignancies” or “blood cancer” or “lymphoma” or “leukemia” or “multiple myeloma.” Additional references were identified through citation tracking of relevant reviews and primary studies, prioritizing the most recent and clinically significant trials, preclinical advances, and mechanistic insights.Inclusion criteria: Studies were included if they evaluated live oncolytic virus platforms specifically targeting hematopoietic malignancies, lymphomas, leukemias, or multiple myeloma in preclinical models or clinical trials. Only articles published in English were considered, with no restrictions applied to publication date or study type.Exclusion criteria: Non-English articles, abstract-only publications lacking primary data, and studies focusing strictly on solid tumors without hematological evaluations were excluded.Initial database searches yielded a combined pool of records. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining articles were screened by the first reviewer based on title and abstract. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies regarding article selection or data extraction were resolved through consensus discussion between both reviewers prior to final inclusion Supplementary Tables and Figure 1. For each eligible study, information regarding study design, disease indication, efficacy-related outcomes, safety profiles, and adverse events associated with oncolytic virotherapy was collected and summarized.Figure 1Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers. Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers recorded in the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases in the past three decades are distributed according to the publication year (X-axis) and virus types (Y-axis). For preclinical studies, the numbers inside the blue circles indicate the number of studies conducted for each OV in that year; those without numbers indicate that only one study was conducted. The Pteropine orthoreovirus (Sikamat virus) grouped under ‘Other’ is a distinct bat-borne species and not the mammalian reovirus (pelareorep) shown as ‘Reovirus’. Detail information was collected in Supplementary Tables 1, 2, from which the figure was generated using Python (Matplotlib).Scatter plot showing years of publication for studies on various oncolytic viruses from 1995 to 2025. Blue circles represent pre-clinical studies, and red stars denote clinical studies or case reports. Each row corresponds to a different virus, including measles virus, adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, reovirus, vaccinia virus, myxoma virus, Newcastle disease virus, herpes simplex virus, and others. Most clinical studies occur after 2015, with recent entries for SARS-CoV-2. A legend specifies the meaning of symbols.
full_text_sections.other: The start: clinical case reports of tumor regressions after virus infectionThe therapeutic potential of viruses in oncology was initially inferred from clinical observations of spontaneous tumor regression following naturally acquired viral infections. Notably, transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma were historically reported during concurrent influenza or measles virus (MV) infections. More recently, similar remissions have been documented in hematologic malignancies following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. The inherent tumor-selectivity demonstrated by many wild-type viruses is largely attributed to the altered cellular landscape of neoplastic cells. Specifically, the hallmarks of cancer create a permissive microenvironment that overlaps significantly with cellular features required for efficient viral replication. Oncolytic viruses: a new generation of live cancer cell killersOVs are replication-competent, biologically active agents that exert anti-cancer effects through two principal mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis and indirect stimulation of systemic anti-tumor immunity. In hematologic malignancies, where cancer cells reside in immune-privileged niches such as the bone marrow or peripheral blood, this dual functionality is particularly advantageous. On one hand, OVs themselves exploit molecular vulnerabilities in malignant cells; on the other hand, OVs can be armed with immunomodulatory transgenes to amplify their therapeutic impact. Pre-clinical studies on evaluating therapeutic OVs in blood cancersTo comprehensively examine and summarize the existing literature regarding OVs in blood cancer therapy and explore treatment-related outcomes, we first retrieved citations using the terms indicated in the Methodology section. After the title and abstract screening phase, the non-overlapping research articles were combined and analyzed. Then we grouped these studies according to the different virus types. Among them, MV was the most frequently studied in publications, followed by adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and reovirus (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Below, we will analyze the study setup and major outcomes of these studies based on different OV types.Although adenovirus was the most frequently applied one in clinical trials,1 only a handful of studies were performed in blood cancer treatment. These studies ranged from systematic evaluation to rational design of human adenoviruses for enhanced blood cancer therapy. In an earlier study by Qian and colleagues, E1B55K-deleted adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) armed with melanoma differentiation-associated gene-7/interleukin-24 (MDA-7/IL-24) was tested in a range of blood cancer cell lines. Although a potent anti-cancer effect was observed in vitro and in vivo, the effect was limited to Ad5 major receptor (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor)-expressing hematological malignancies (Qian et al., 2008). Follow-up studies solved the problem by using chimeric Ad35 fiber (Wang et al., 2009; Wenthe et al., 2020). Another study compared the growth-inhibition effect of adenovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV) on several cell lines; HSV was more effective (Zhang et al., 2011). Realizing the limitation from Ad5, a broad range of human adenoviruses were evaluated by Barry’s research group. They observed robust killing and delayed lymphoma growth by species D adenoviruses (Chen et al., 2011). However, in mouse B cell lymphoma model A20, only prophylactic immunization by adenovirus against A20 tumors can protect against A20 lymphomas; established A20 tumors were not controlled by A20-expressing adenovirus immunization (Weaver et al., 2011). While OV alone is not enough to control blood malignancies, a combination approach highlights the optimized development strategy. A rationally designed OAd5F35, Ad5-based chimeric virus with Ad35 fiber, armed with TMZ-CD40L and 4-1BBL was evaluated in combination with CAR-T therapy. The fiber switch to Ad35 enabled the use of CD46, which is up-regulated in hematological malignancies, thereby enhancing targeting and replication. Interestingly, OAd5F35 infection induced transgene expression and a change in immune markers. In combination with CAR-T therapy, the infected lymphoma cells were found to secrete chemokines to attract CAR-T cells, thereby increased CAR-T cell activation was observed. Importantly, the enhanced lymphoma cell killing was also observed in vivo in xenograft models (Wenthe et al., 2021). Similarly, a CD47 antibody expressing adenovirus (Ad5-hTert-E1A-IRES-E1B with mCMV-mCD47nb-Fc) as in situ tumor vaccination also showed positive immune-regulation and protection from tumor re-challenge (Zhang et al., 2022). These data suggested that adenovirus alone is not enough to control such aggressive hematological malignancies; a combination approach should be the development strategy of choice.Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), based on HSV-1, is so far the only OV approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of melanoma (Zhang T. et al., 2023). However, only a few studies have explored its potential in hematological malignancies. In the search for molecular indicators for permissiveness to HSV therapy, transcription factors downstream of Ras were evaluated in non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) cell lines infected with R3616, an HSV-1 with a deletion of the viral γ134.5 gene. Ras signaling was assessed by immunoblotting for different downstream effectors, which revealed ERK/ELK as a suitable predictive indicator for selection of cancer cells with increased sensitivity to HSV-based therapy (Esfandyari et al., 2009). As G47Δ was approved in Japan in 2021 (Frampton, 2022), a similar version of this OV was evaluated in a broad panel of 26 cell lines and 15 primary cells derived from various lineages of hematological malignancies (Ishino et al., 2021). The expression of an HSV-1 receptor, nectin-1, was identified as a determining factor in the oncolytic effect determined by viral entry and cytotoxicity. Although only a low level of virus replication was detected in hematological cancer cells, the virus could induce immunogenic cell death and kill the malignant cells. Importantly, this study demonstrated that systemic tumor-specific CD8 + T cell responses efficiently concentrated at tumor sites, suggesting that local intratumoral injection of HSV-1 is expected to provoke effective immune responses even for systemic tumors such as hematological malignancies. Recently, an oncolytic type II HSV (oHSV2) was explored in the treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (Zhang J. et al., 2023). In comparison with the clinical chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin (DOX), oHSV2 revealed a better therapeutic profile on the apoptotic, invasive, and proliferative capacity of DLBCL cells in vitro. Moreover, oHSV2 can also inhibit transplanted tumor growth and accelerate CD4 + T and CD8 + T cell infiltration in mice, with an acceptable safety profile in the organs of tumor-bearing animals. To explore the potential of combination therapy with immune-checkpoint inhibitors, this study also showed oHSV2 can inhibit the PD-1/PD-L1 immune-checkpoint, thereby restraining cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) apoptosis and encouraging CTL proliferation. The combination therapy resulted in enhanced killing of malignant cells and inhibited tumor growth in mice. Similar to the adenovirus studies, combination therapy and the individual receptor profile are essential for further HSV application in hematological malignancies.The rat protoparvovirus H-1 (H-1PV) does not infect or cause any disease in humans, but has natural tropism for human cancer cells. H-1PV demonstrates a broad range of anticancer activities in several preclinical cancer models and in clinical trials (Geletneky et al., 2017; Bretscher and Marchini, 2019; Hajda et al., 2021). analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies, highlighting the need for systemic targeting strategies due to the limitations of existing treatments for relapsed or refractory diseases.

analysis.methods: The review involved a systematic search of databases, screening of articles by title and abstract, and full-text assessment by two independent reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus discussion, and data on study design, disease indication, efficacy, safety, and adverse events were collected and summarized.
analysis.main_results: Clinical case reports documented transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma during concurrent influenza or measles virus infections. Additionally, similar remissions were observed in hematologic malignancies following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as evidence of the inherent tumor-selectivity of wild-type viruses, which is attributed to the cancer cell microenvironment overlapping with viral replication requirements. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that oncolytic viruses could offer innovative therapeutic options for hematopoietic malignancies, particularly for patients with relapsed or refractory disease who may not benefit from current treatments.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in treating hematopoietic malignancies, emphasizing their unique advantages in systemic targeting. The study highlights the limitations of current treatments like autologous stem cell transplantation and CAR T-cell therapy, which are constrained by logistical and financial challenges. By analyzing over 100 preclinical studies and multiple early-phase clinical trials, the authors propose three development pathways to enhance the clinical viability of oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology. The findings suggest that viruses such as influenza and measles may induce transient remissions in certain hematologic malignancies, potentially due to the permissive microenvironment of cancer cells. However, the study is limited to a literature review and does not include original data, resulting in moderate evidence strength. The results underscore the need for further research into oncolytic virotherapy as a promising alternative for advanced hematologic cancers.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估溶瘤病毒在造血系统恶性肿瘤中的治疗潜力,强调由于现有 治疗 对于复发或难治性疾病的局限性,需要采用系统靶向策略。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 通过搜索 PubMed 和 ClinicalTrials.gov 截至 2026 年 7 月,使用与溶瘤病毒和造血系统恶性肿瘤相关的特定术语进行了小型审查。纳入标准侧重于在临床前模型或临床试验中评估针对这些恶性肿瘤的活溶瘤病毒平台的研究。
elements_zh.methods: 该审查涉及对数据库的系统检索、按标题和摘要筛选文章以及由两名独立审稿人进行全文评估。通过共识讨论解决分歧,并收集和总结有关研究设计、疾病适应症、疗效、安全性和不良事件的数据。
elements_zh.main_results: 临床 病例报告 记录了白血病和淋巴瘤患者在并发流感或麻疹病毒感染期间的短暂缓解。此外,在感染 SARS-CoV-2 后的血液恶性肿瘤中也观察到类似的缓解。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为野生型病毒固有的肿瘤选择性的证据,这归因于癌细胞微环境与病毒复制要求重叠。这代表了溶瘤病毒疗法治疗血液恶性肿瘤的治疗潜力的新视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,溶瘤病毒可以为造血系统恶性肿瘤提供创新的治疗选择,特别是对于可能无法从当前的 治疗 中受益的复发或难治性疾病患者。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于对现有文献的回顾,不包括原始数据。证据强度中等,因为它依赖于历史 病例报告 和临床前研究,而不是大规模临床试验。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估溶瘤病毒在造血系统恶性肿瘤中的治疗潜力,强调由于现有 治疗 对于复发或难治性疾病的局限性,需要采用系统靶向策略。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 通过搜索 PubMed 和 ClinicalTrials.gov 截至 2026 年 7 月,使用与溶瘤病毒和造血系统恶性肿瘤相关的特定术语进行了小型审查。纳入标准侧重于在临床前模型或临床试验中评估针对这些恶性肿瘤的活溶瘤病毒平台的研究。
analysis_zh.methods: 该审查涉及对数据库的系统检索、按标题和摘要筛选文章以及由两名独立审稿人进行全文评估。通过共识讨论解决分歧,并收集和总结有关研究设计、疾病适应症、疗效、安全性和不良事件的数据。
analysis_zh.main_results: 临床 病例报告 记录了白血病和淋巴瘤患者在并发流感或麻疹病毒感染期间的短暂缓解。此外,在感染 SARS-CoV-2 后的血液恶性肿瘤中也观察到类似的缓解。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为野生型病毒固有的肿瘤选择性的证据,这归因于癌细胞微环境与病毒复制要求重叠。这代表了溶瘤病毒疗法治疗血液恶性肿瘤的治疗潜力的新视角。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,溶瘤病毒可以为造血系统恶性肿瘤提供创新的治疗选择,特别是对于可能无法从当前的 治疗 中受益的复发或难治性疾病患者。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于对现有文献的回顾,不包括原始数据。证据强度中等,因为它依赖于历史 病例报告 和临床前研究,而不是大规模临床试验。

papers.title: Upper respiratory virome signatures reflect COVID-19 severity and post-recovery shifts
papers.abstract: Introduction Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection profoundly affects the upper respiratory tract, yet the dynamics of the resident virome across different stages of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) and recovery remain poorly understood. Methods This study profiled alterations in the virome and microbiome in 143 SARS-CoV-2–positive adults, stratified by disease severity (Non-Severe, Severe, Critical), compared with 96 RT-PCR–negative controls. Nasal and oral swabs underwent targeted viral enrichment and next-generation sequencing, followed by virome profiling. Results The respiratory virome of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals was dominated by SARS-CoV-2, with co-detected viruses such as Human Mastadenovirus C, which increased with disease severity and persisting post-recovery. Alpha diversity was highest in Non-Severe cases and declined in Severe and Critical groups, suggesting increasing disruption of the virome with disease severity. Beta diversity showed clear separation between controls and cases, and across severity levels. LEfSe identified distinct viral signatures differentiating infection status, and logistic regression of key viral taxa accurately classified Critical versus post-recovery samples (AUC = 0.91). Although the study focused on viruses, bacterial taxa including Rothia mucilaginosa and Haemophilus parahaemolyticus were also detected with severity-linked variation, highlighting viral–bacterial interactions. Longitudinal paired analysis revealed consistent post-recovery enrichment of Streptococcus-specific bacteriophages across all severity groups, suggesting restoration of Streptococcus-associated phage dynamics during convalescence. Discussion Overall, this study reveals SARS-CoV-2–associated alterations in the respiratory virome and microbiome and highlights specific microbial taxa with potential as biomarkers for disease severity and post-infection recovery.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨不同阶段的 COVID-19 和康复过程中上呼吸道病毒组的变化,因为这些阶段的常驻病毒组动态尚未被充分理解。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了143名SARS-CoV-2阳性成人,按疾病严重程度分为非严重、严重和危重组,并与96名RT-PCR阴性对照进行了比较。
elements_zh.methods: 鼻咽拭子经过靶向病毒富集和下一代测序,随后进行病毒组分析。使用LEfSe识别独特的病毒特征,并对关键病毒类群进行逻辑回归分析以分类危重组与康复后样本。
elements_zh.main_results: SARS-CoV-2阳性个体的呼吸道病毒组主要由SARS-CoV-2主导,伴随检测到的病毒如人腺病毒C(Human Mastadenovirus C)在疾病严重程度增加时增多,并在康复后持续存在。β多样性显示对照组与病例组之间以及不同严重程度组之间存在明显的分离。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为揭示了SARS-CoV-2与呼吸道病毒组和微生物组相关的改变,并指出某些微生物类群可能作为疾病严重程度和感染后康复的生物标志物。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能有助于开发评估疾病严重程度和监测感染后病毒组变化的生物标志物,从而可能有助于制定针对性的监测和干预策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据强度中等,因为它主要关注病毒和细菌类群,而未明确探讨因果关系或长期影响,且研究结果的普遍适用性可能受到限制。

papers.abstract_zh: 引言 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒-2(SARS-CoV-2)感染对上呼吸道有显著影响,但 Coronavirus Disease 2019(COVID-19)及其康复阶段的常驻病毒组动态仍不明确。方法 本研究分析了143名SARS-CoV-2阳性成人(按疾病严重程度分为非严重、严重和危重组),并与96名RT-PCR阴性对照进行了比较。鼻咽拭子经过靶向病毒富集和下一代测序,随后进行病毒组分析。结果 SARS-CoV-2阳性个体的呼吸道病毒组主要由SARS-CoV-2主导,伴随检测到的病毒如人腺病毒C(Human Mastadenovirus C)在疾病严重程度增加时增多,并在康复后持续存在。α多样性在非严重病例中最高,而在严重和危重组中下降,表明随着疾病严重程度的增加,病毒组的紊乱程度增加。β多样性显示对照组与病例组之间以及不同严重程度组之间存在明显的分离。LEfSe识别出区分感染状态的病毒特征,关键病毒类群的逻辑回归分析准确分类了危重组与康复后样本(AUC = 0.91)。尽管本研究主要关注病毒,但也检测到与严重程度相关的细菌类群,如Rothia mucilaginosa和Haemophilus parahaemolyticus,突显了病毒与细菌之间的相互作用。纵向配对分析显示,在所有严重程度组中,康复后均一致富集了链球菌特异性噬菌体,表明在康复期链球菌相关噬菌体动态可能得到恢复。讨论 总体而言,本研究揭示了SARS-CoV-2与呼吸道病毒组和微生物组相关的改变,并突出了某些微生物类群作为疾病严重程度和感染后康复的生物标志物的潜力。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨不同阶段的 COVID-19 和康复过程中上呼吸道病毒组的变化,因为这些阶段的常驻病毒组动态尚未被充分理解。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了143名SARS-CoV-2阳性成人,按疾病严重程度分为非严重、严重和危重组,并与96名RT-PCR阴性对照进行了比较。
analysis_zh.methods: 鼻咽拭子经过靶向病毒富集和下一代测序,随后进行病毒组分析。使用LEfSe识别独特的病毒特征,并对关键病毒类群进行逻辑回归分析以分类危重组与康复后样本。
analysis_zh.main_results: SARS-CoV-2阳性个体的呼吸道病毒组主要由SARS-CoV-2主导,伴随检测到的病毒如人腺病毒C(Human Mastadenovirus C)在疾病严重程度增加时增多,并在康复后持续存在。β多样性显示对照组与病例组之间以及不同严重程度组之间存在明显的分离。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为揭示了SARS-CoV-2与呼吸道病毒组和微生物组相关的改变,并指出某些微生物类群可能作为疾病严重程度和感染后康复的生物标志物。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能有助于开发评估疾病严重程度和监测感染后病毒组变化的生物标志物,从而可能有助于制定针对性的监测和干预策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据强度中等,因为它主要关注病毒和细菌类群,而未明确探讨因果关系或长期影响,且研究结果的普遍适用性可能受到限制。

papers.full_text: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. MATERIALS AND METHODSCollection and purification of LCTG-001SIgA was purified and pooled from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals, as described previously (13). Briefly, frozen human milk was thawed and clarified through centrifugation and dialyzed in PBS. The supernatant was loaded onto a CaptureSelect IgA Affinity Matrix resin, and IgA was isolated as previously described (13). Pooled elution fractions were dialyzed in PBS and filtered. The final concentration was determined using a spectrophotometer.SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresisTwo micrograms of LCTG-001 was mixed with 4× lithium dodecyl sulfate loading dye and β-mercaptoethanol at 95°C for 10 min. Sample was loaded onto a 4 to 12% bis-tris gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ran at 100 V for 90 min with Bolt Mops SDS running buffer (Invitrogen). The gel was stained with Coomassie blue for 30 min at room temperature and destained using 40% methanol and 10% acetic acid in water.Neutrophil isolationNeutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood of consenting healthy male and female donors as described previously, using density gradient centrifugation (29, 30). Studies were approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board. Briefly, blood was collected into EDTA-coated tubes via venipuncture. Three milliliters of Histopaque 1119 and 3 ml of Histopaque 1077 were layered in a 15-ml Falcon tube, followed by 6 ml of blood. Samples were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 30 min at room temperature with no deceleration in an Allegra X-12R centrifuge (Beckman Coulter). The neutrophil layer was collected between the Histopaque layers and red blood cells (RBCs). Neutrophils were diluted in 50 ml of cold polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) buffer [0.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.3 mM EDTA (Invitrogen) in Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco)]. Diluted cells were centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

full_text_sections.results: RESULTSAssessment of broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogensUnlike IgG in conventional IVIG or convalescent plasma, which is peripherally sourced from the circulation, SIgA is exclusively found at mucosal sites. Sourcing from the respiratory mucosa is not feasible due to procedural complexities and limited antibody yield. To circumvent these limitations, we explored breast milk as an alternative source of mucosal SIgA. Breast milk is a scalable and sustainable source of mucosal SIgA, and donations of extra breast milk are already collected by over 700 human milk banks worldwide. To produce purified SIgA, breast milk samples were collected from 120 lactating donors through collaborations with milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Initial sample shipments included 85 donor contributions received on 11 October 2022, followed by an additional 35 samples on 29 November 2022. The samples, collected throughout 2022, were pooled to yield a total volume of 15,585 ml. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. The purity of LCTG-001 was confirmed by Coomassie staining (fig. S1) and was consistent with previous reports (13). The donor cohort was not screened for recent infection or vaccination status, thereby aligning with conventional IVIG collection practices in which donors are not selected on the basis of prior antigenic exposures (3, 14).We next evaluated whether the polyclonal SIgA pool, LCTG-001, could recognize and neutralize a panel of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus (HuAd), and IAV. Representative strains and serotypes were selected for each virus to assess LCTG-001’s binding and neutralizing potency. To assess LCTG-001’s antiviral activity, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to evaluate antibody binding, alongside microneutralization (MNT) assays to measure functional neutralization.We first assessed binding of LCTG-001 to RSV fusion protein (RSV-F), the antigen used in licensed RSV vaccines (15). LCTG-001 demonstrated robust binding to RSV-F (AUC = 62.02 ± 1.273; Fig. 1A), and these antibodies were able to neutralize RSV at physiologically relevant concentrations [median inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 320 μg/ml; Fig. 1B].Fig. 1.LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogens.(A, C, and E) LCTG-001 binding responses to RSV-F (A), HuAd5 lysate (C), and Cal/09 HA (E). (B, D, and F) LCTG-001 neutralizing antibody responses to RSV (B), HuAd5 (D), and Cal/09 (F), measured by percent (%) neutralization using MNT assays. Data presented in (A) to (F) represent mean ± SEM. Data presented in (A), (C), and (E) represent three technical replicates. Data presented in (B), (D), and (F) are from three independent experiments.We next assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against adenovirus, focusing on HuAd type 5 (HuAd5), one of the most prevalent HuAd serotypes (16, 17). ELISAs were performed using the lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells as a source of antigen (18). Again, LCTG-001 demonstrated specific binding to the lysate of infected cells (AUC = 62.28 ± 2.309; Fig. 1C) and neutralized HuAd5 with considerable potency (IC50 = 180 μg/ml; Fig. 1D).Last, we assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against IAV. IAV is a respiratory virus responsible for both seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics, with five pandemics in the last century (19). We first investigated the ability of LCTG-001 to recognize and neutralize A/California/07/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09). Cal/09 (H1N1) is an isolate from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which then circulated seasonally and was a recommended seasonal influenza vaccine strain for more than 5 years in North America. Hence, most of the population has been exposed through infection and/or vaccination. Similar to RSV and HuAd5, LCTG-001 showed specific binding to Cal/09 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA) (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E) and neutralization activity (IC50 = 670 μg/ml; Fig. 1F). Together, these findings demonstrate that LCTG-001, a breast milk–derived polyclonal SIgA product, exhibits broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple clinically relevant respiratory pathogens.LCTG-001 engages nonneutralizing antibody effector functions against H1N1 IAVWhile vaccination remains the primary strategy for control of seasonal influenza, antigenic drift, particularly in the HA head domain, limits vaccine effectiveness and necessitates regular vaccine strain updates. Antibody responses generated by infection or vaccination primarily target the immunodominant HA head, which can significantly vary between strains. Unlike the variable HA head, the stalk domain is relatively conserved, with stalk-specific antibodies capable of providing protection against diverse IAV strains (20). However, stalk-specific antibody responses are typically low in magnitude but tend to increase with age and influenza virus exposures (21, 22). Despite this, these antibodies can provide broad protection by targeting conserved stalk epitopes, particularly in the context of vaccine mismatch or exposure to novel pandemic strains where HA head-specific immunity is lacking. Hence, we next sought to determine whether stalk-specific anti-IAV antibodies were present in LCTG-001 through the use of a chimeric HA protein (cH6/1) composed of the conserved stalk domain of A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) and the head domain from the avian A/mallard/Sweden/81/02 (H6N2) strain (23). The use of an avian H6 head, which is rarely encountered in humans, allows for measurement of stalk-specific binding antibodies (24). Using this approach, LCTG-001 demonstrated stalk-specific binding antibody responses (AUC = 46.35 ± 9.036; Fig. 2A) that were not statistically different (P = 0.54) from antibody responses to full-length Cal/09 (H1N1) HA (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E), suggesting that a large proportion of H1 HA-specific antibodies present in LCTG-001 recognizes the H1 stalk.
